simba.Codes.MADX package

Submodules

simba.Codes.MADX.MADX module

SIMBA MAD-X Module

Various objects and functions to handle MAD-X lattices and tracking. The interaction with MAD-X is handled through the cpymad library, which embeds the MAD-X interpreter in the Python process; see the MAD-X manual for details of the underlying commands.

The lattice (including explicit drifts) is converted into one or more MAD-X SEQUENCE blocks via the LAURA SectionLatticeTranslator machinery. Since MAD-X reference momentum is fixed for a given BEAM statement (magnet strengths are normalised to it, and tracking coordinates are canonical w.r.t. it), the lattice is split into segments at each accelerating (RF) cavity. Each segment is tracked with the local reference momentum taken from the tracked bunch itself, and the particle coordinates are re-referenced between segments – mirroring the always_change_p0 behaviour used for ELEGANT and the internal energy bookkeeping of Ocelot, so that the beam evolution can be interpreted in the same way as for the other tracking codes.

Two tracking modes are available:

  • Full-beam tracking (default): every macro-particle in the input distribution is tracked with the thin-lens tracking module (TRACK … START … RUN), and output beam distributions are written (in OpenPMD HDF5 format) at every diagnostic (Screen, Marker and BPM) in the lattice, as well as at the end of the line.

  • single_particle mode: only the beam centroid (plus a small set of probe trajectories used to build the linear map by finite differences) is tracked through each segment with standard MAD-X tracking. The output beam at every diagnostic, and at the end of the line, is then generated by applying the resulting transformation (centroid + linear map) to the initial particle distribution.

In both cases a Twiss summary file (<lattice>_twiss.madx.hdf5) is written, containing both the MAD-X model optics (Twiss functions, dispersion, phase advances) and beam-distribution statistics (momentum, sizes, bunch length, emittances), which can be loaded through simba.Modules.Twiss.load_directory() in the same way as the output of the other tracking codes.

Classes:

  • madxLattice: The MAD-X lattice object, used for converting the elements defined in the frameworkLattice into MAD-X sequences, and for tracking through them using cpymad.

class madxLattice(**data)[source]

Bases: frameworkLattice

Class for defining the MAD-X lattice object, used for converting the elements defined in the frameworkLattice into MAD-X SEQUENCE definitions and for tracking through them with cpymad.

The lattice is split into segments at each RF cavity so that the MAD-X reference momentum (to which magnet strengths and canonical track coordinates are normalised) can follow the acceleration of the beam; the particle coordinates are transformed between the segment-local reference frames via the generic beam object.

If single_particle is False (the default), the full particle distribution is tracked and beam distributions are written at each diagnostic (Screen, Marker and BPM) in the lattice. If True, standard (single-particle) MAD-X tracking is performed for the beam centroid and a set of probe trajectories, and only the output beam at the end of the line is generated, based on a transformation (centroid offset plus finite-difference linear map) of the initial distribution.

Parameters:

data (Any)

beam_data: Dict

Data containing beam statistics at each observation point

cavity_model: str

Transverse model for accelerating (RF) cavities:

  • rsmatrix (default): the transverse motion through the structure is described by a first-order MAD-X MATRIX element containing the Rosenzweig-Serafini accelerating-structure matrix (as also used by Ocelot), which accounts for adiabatic damping and ponderomotive (RF) focusing; the energy gain and RF curvature are applied by a thin RFCAVITY kick. In the fixed-reference-momentum canonical coordinates of a segment this matrix is exactly symplectic.

  • sliced: the cavity is subdivided into nslice_rfcavity thin RF kicks with exact drifts in between (adiabatic damping only).

  • thin: a single thin RF kick at the centre of the structure (the plain MAD-X MAKETHIN treatment).

Notes

Cached per segment, because the turn loop asks for this once a turn and the answer cannot change during a run: it is the set of zero-length diagnostics and their s positions, and a device program varies an element’s strength through MAD-X input, never the element set or the geometry. Recomputing it was ~20% of the per-turn cost of a tracking run – screens_and_markers_and_bpms is a property that rebuilds and re-sorts three getElementType queries, and sorting on physical.start.z pulls each element through LAURA’s cascading attribute resolution every time.

zeta = beta0 * t and delta = pt / beta0, so R56 picks up beta0**2.

static rescale_twiss_init(init, ratio)[source]

Re-reference a set of Twiss functions from one MAD-X reference momentum to another (ratio = p0c_new / p0c_old).

The MAD-X Twiss functions are defined in the canonical coordinates (x, px = Px/P0) of the segment, so they depend on the segment reference momentum. Since the beam is accelerated by the cavity at the end of each segment, the reference momentum changes at every segment boundary and the Twiss functions have to be transformed accordingly.

  • ratio (float)

run_segments(madx)[source]

Track through each lattice segment in turn; see run().

A line asking for several turns repeats the whole segment sweep, the beam leaving the last segment re-entering the first. Which turns are recorded is output_turns().

A run that does not need Python between turns is handed to MAD-X whole instead; use_native_turns() is the test and run_segments_native() is the path.

Parameters:

madx (Any)

Return type:

None

run_segments_native(madx)[source]

Track the whole multi-turn run in one MAD-X RUN.

The alternative to run_segments()’ Python turn loop, used when use_native_turns() says nothing needs to happen between one turn and the next. MAD-X is asked for every turn at once and leaves a single trackone table holding each recorded turn at every observation point; the per-turn work simba would have done becomes one pass over that table afterwards.

Two things make this bounded rather than merely fast. FFILE (see run_track()) means only the turns output_turns() asks for are ever put in the table, so its size follows the output request and not the turn count. And the reference momentum is constant here by construction – one segment means no boundary at which it could be re-referenced – so the per-turn momentum bookkeeping the loop does has nothing to do.

A superperiod is still a pass and not a turn: MAD-X is asked for turns * passes_per_turn of them, and simba’s turn t is MAD-X’s turn t * passes_per_turn.

Parameters:

madx (Any)

Return type:

None

run_track(madx, coords, observe, numbers=None, turns=1, ffile=1)[source]

Run the MAD-X thin-lens tracking module (TRACK/START/ OBSERVE/RUN/ENDTRACK) for one segment and return the contents of the trackone table.

Parameters:

  • madx (cpymad.madx.Madx) – The MAD-X instance

  • coords (Dict) – The canonical starting coordinates

  • observe (List) – (name, s) tuples at which to observe the beam

  • numbers (np.ndarray, optional) – Particle numbers to assign (defaults to 1..N)

  • turns (int) – How many turns to ask MAD-X for in one RUN. 1 is the segmented path, which does its own turn loop in Python; run_segments_native() passes the whole run.

  • ffile (int) – Record only every ffile-th turn. This is what keeps the native path’s memory flat: trackone holds every recorded turn at every observation point, so at 512 particles storing all of them costs ~2M rows and 457 MB per 1000 turns and grows without limit, while storing every 2000th of 20 000 turns is 21k rows and 47 MB. output_turns() already says which turns are wanted, and this is how MAD-X is told.

Returns:

Dictionary of arrays from the MAD-X trackone table

Return type:

Dict

segmentElements()[source]

Split the lattice (including explicit drifts) into segments, breaking after each RF cavity. Within each segment the beam energy – and therefore the MAD-X reference momentum – is constant, which allows normalised magnet strengths to be interpreted at the local design momentum, in the same way as for the other supported tracking codes.

A ring is left as one segment; segment_at_cavities() says why.

Returns:

A list of segments, each a list of element names (in order).

Return type:

List

property segment_at_cavities: bool

Whether RF cavities should break the lattice into segments.

They should on a linac, which is what the splitting is for: an accelerating cavity moves the beam energy, MAD-X’s reference momentum is fixed for a given BEAM statement, and normalised strengths and canonical coordinates are both defined against it. Splitting lets each segment be tracked at its own momentum.

They should not on a ring. A storage-ring cavity does not move the reference energy, it holds the beam at it; the motion it drives is a synchrotron oscillation about the synchronous phase, which MAD-X tracks on its own. Measured on a 16-bend ring with a real cavity, the longitudinal amplitude drifts by +0.003% over 20 000 turns and -0.07% over 100 000, and the synchrotron tune scales as the square root of the voltage, as it should.

Splitting such a ring is not merely unnecessary, it is what forces the slow path: a segment boundary is a hand-back to Python, so a split ring cannot use MAD-X’s own RUN, TURNS=N and pays simba’s per-turn cost instead (see run_segments_native()). Not splitting leaves a one-segment ring, which can.

closed_geometry() and not periodic, so that an injection study asking for the open optics solution on a real ring does not thereby re-acquire accelerating cavities.

The flag itself lives on single_particle() – it was a MAD-X field until R1, and the concept is code-independent.

property use_native_turns: bool

Whether this run can hand the whole turn loop to MAD-X.

MAD-X tracks multiple turns itself, and does it far faster than simba can drive it one turn at a time: at 512 particles the Python loop costs ~12 ms a turn, where RUN, TURNS=20000 on the same lattice is 0.8 s in total. The loop exists because of the things below, not because the turn count has to be in Python.

The conditions, each of which needs Python between turns:

  • more than one segment. A segment boundary re-references the beam momentum, so the turn has to come back to simba. With segment_at_cavities() a ring is one segment, so in practice this excludes linacs, which do not have turns anyway.

  • device programs. A program varies an element per turn (apply_programs()), which is a MAD-X input statement between one turn and the next.

  • single-particle mode, which is not one tracking run at all: it builds each segment’s linear map by finite differences and applies it to the distribution.

  • native_turns: false, the explicit override. It belongs in the tracking block, beside the turn count it is about:

    files:
  RING:
    code: madx
    tracking: {turns: 1000, native_turns: false}

    and falls back to the MAD-X setting of the same name, so it can also be turned off globally.

Returns:

True if run_segments_native() should be used

Return type:

bool
